short: A clear role, a specific instruction stated early, relevant context separated by delimiters, representative examples where helpful, and an explicit output format; then testing on a set of cases.
Zero-shot gives only an instruction; few-shot adds k input–output examples so the model infers format and decision boundaries from context.
A model's ability to perform a task specified by examples in its prompt without any weight updates, emerging in large pre-trained models.
Sample multiple reasoning paths/answers with temperature > 0 and output the most frequent final answer.
Splitting a task into a sequence of prompts where each step's output becomes the next step's input, making each step simpler and checkable.
Tools are described with names and JSON schemas; the model returns a structured call when needed; the application validates and executes it and returns the result for the model's final answer.
Restricting generation so only tokens consistent with a grammar, regex or JSON schema can be sampled (others masked to zero probability), guaranteeing valid structured output.

q: How do example choice and order affect few-shot results?
short: Label imbalance biases outputs; recency bias weighs later examples; semantically similar examples (retrieved per query) help; correct format matters even more than label correctness in some studies.
When the model is usually wrong (p < 0.5), when errors are correlated (same misconception each time), for open-ended outputs without a canonical answer, or when cost/latency budgets are tight.

q: Make a prompt robust for a production extraction task.
short: Explicit schema and examples, delimiters around input, instructions to use null for missing fields, constrained decoding or validation with retries, a test suite of edge cases, version control and monitoring.
mistakes: Parsing free text with regex afterwards.

short: Using an LLM to propose candidate instructions (from examples or by mutating existing prompts), scoring them on a validation set, and iterating to find a high-performing prompt.

q: Prompting vs fine-tuning for a new task?
short: Prompting: no training, instant iteration, uses context tokens, may be less consistent. Fine-tuning: consistent behaviour, shorter prompts, needs data and training, harder to update. Start with prompting.

q: Why put instructions before data and use delimiters?
short: Models give weight to early instructions, and delimiters mark untrusted content as data, reducing confusion and prompt-injection risk when documents contain instruction-like text.
mistakes: Concatenating user text into the instruction.

short: Yes: forcing a strict format early can stop the model from reasoning or push it into low-probability tokens; mitigate by letting it reason first then emit the structured answer, or using a schema with a reasoning field.

q: Design tool calling for a banking assistant.
short: Read-only tools by default; strict schemas; server-side validation and authorisation per user; confirmations for any money movement; rate limits; logging; treat tool outputs as data; never let model output directly authorise transactions.
mistakes: Letting the model call transfer without confirmation.

q: Why does in-context learning work at all?
short: Hypotheses: pre-training on documents with repeated patterns teaches the model to infer latent tasks; attention can implement simple learning algorithms (e.g. induction heads copying patterns, gradient-descent-like updates) in its forward pass.

q: Self-consistency budget: p = 0.6, target 0.8 majority accuracy. Minimum odd n?
Build an evaluation harness for prompts.
short: Curate a representative test set with edge cases, define automatic metrics and LLM-judge rubrics, run every prompt version, track accuracy, format validity, cost and latency, and gate deployments on regressions.

q: How do structured outputs interact with tokenization?
short: Grammar states are over characters but models emit tokens spanning several characters; engines must precompute which tokens are valid from each state, and token boundaries can make some valid strings awkward or improbable.
